claims.text: Aortic arch: three major branches: the brachiocephalic artery, left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery.
claims.quote: There are three major branches of the aortic arch: the brachiocephalic artery, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian (literally “under the clavicle”) artery.

claims.text: Common carotids: the right arises from the brachiocephalic artery, the left from the aortic arch; each gives rise to the external and internal carotid arteries.
claims.quote: The right common carotid artery arises from the brachiocephalic artery and the left common carotid artery arises from the aortic arch; each gives rise to the external and internal carotid arteries; supplies the respective sides of the head and neck
claims.locator: Table: Aortic Arch Branches and Brain Circulation

claims.text: External carotid: supplies the face, lower jaw, neck, esophagus and larynx.
claims.quote: External carotid artery Arises from the common carotid artery; supplies blood to numerous structures within the face, lower jaw, neck, esophagus, and larynx
claims.locator: Table: Aortic Arch Branches and Brain Circulation

claims.text: Internal carotid: begins with the carotid sinus, passes through the carotid canal of the temporal bone and supplies the brain.
claims.quote: Internal carotid artery Arises from the common carotid artery and begins with the carotid sinus; goes through the carotid canal of the temporal bone to the base of the brain; combines with the branches of the vertebral artery, forming the arterial circle; supplies blood to the brain
claims.locator: Table: Aortic Arch Branches and Brain Circulation

claims.text: Vertebral artery: branches from the subclavian artery and runs through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae to the skull base.
claims.quote: The vertebral artery branches from the subclavian artery and passes through the transverse foramen in the cervical vertebrae, entering the base of the skull at the vertebral foramen.

claims.text: Thyrocervical artery: from the subclavian; supplies the thyroid, the neck, and the upper back and shoulder.
claims.quote: The subclavian artery also gives rise to the thyrocervical artery that provides blood to the thyroid, the cervical region of the neck, and the upper back and shoulder.

claims.text: Internal jugular vein: runs with the common carotid, mainly drains the brain, and empties into the subclavian vein.
claims.quote: Internal jugular vein Parallel to the common carotid artery, which is more or less its counterpart, and passes through the jugular foramen and canal; primarily drains blood from the brain, receives the superficial facial vein, and empties into the subclavian vein
claims.locator: Table: Major Veins of the Head and Neck

claims.text: External jugular vein: drains the superficial head, scalp and cranial regions into the subclavian vein.
claims.quote: External jugular vein Drains blood from the more superficial portions of the head, scalp, and cranial regions, and leads to the subclavian vein
claims.locator: Table: Major Veins of the Head and Neck

claims.text: Anterior nosebleeds: most nasal bleeding; from a plexus of vessels on the anteroinferior septum (Kiesselbach area).
claims.quote: Most nasal bleeding is anterior, originating from a plexus of vessels in the anteroinferior septum (Kiesselbach area).

claims.text: Posterior nosebleeds: less common but more serious; from the posterior septum over the vomer or laterally from the inferior or middle turbinate.
claims.quote: Less common but more serious are posterior nosebleeds, which originate in the posterior septum overlying the vomer bone or laterally from the inferior or middle turbinate.

claims.text: Arteries ligated: the internal maxillary (through the maxillary sinus) or the sphenopalatine (transnasal endoscopic).
claims.quote: The arteries may be ligated with clips using endoscopic or microscopic guidance and a surgical approach through the maxillary sinus (internal maxillary) or transnasal endoscopic approach (sphenopalatine).
